analytic.title: A Generalized Utilization Bound Test for Fixed-Priority Real-Time Scheduling

div.p: Liu and Layland provided a utilization bound test which is applicable to rate-monotonic priority assignment, when all tasks deadlines are at the end of their periods. Subsequently, Lehoczky and others provided an ezact schedulability criterion which is applicable to any arbitrary priority assignment scheme, with no restriction on task deadlines, which can be used when all task computation times are known exactly. In this work, we fill an important gap between these two, b y presenting a technique for deriving utilization bounds, based on linear programming, that is applicable to similarly generalized situations, but does not require knowledge of exact task computation times.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The rate-monotonic scheduling algorithm, introduced by Liu and Layland [l was subsequently modified by Sha, Lehoczky and ot k ers [3,4,5]. In this work, we develop a technique to determine the utilization bound for a specific task sei, where we know the period and deadline of each of the tasks, but we may not have complete information about task computation times. This problem is an important one in the design of real-time systems, since task periods and deadlines depend on the characteristics of the application and are usually fixed at design-time, whereas computation times are very difficult to determine, even after the actual application code has been written. The computation to be performed may vary from one arrival to the next (it may be data-dependent); various system features, such as interrupts, cache memory, virtual memory, I/O, message transmission over networks, resource availability may all cause variations in the execution time of tasks. This difficulty is usually overcome by determining an upper bound on S. Natarajan Xerox Corp. 1350 Jefferson Rd.

However, it may not even be possible to determine a useful worst-case bound in many applications, such as radar tracking, where the computation time depends directly on the number of objects being tracked. Therefore, it would be very useful to determine a utilization bound which takes into account the specific task periods, but does not make assumptions about task computation times for those applications.
A utilization bound has the advantage over an exact schedulability criterion since it can be used to perform simple schedulability checks at run-time, when tasks may have transient overloads.

In addition to being able to derive a task set-specific utilization bound when the period, deadline and priority assignment are known, our work can also take advantage of any information about the maximum and/or minimum computation time for each task, if they are bounded at design time. In general, computation time analysis may not be able to produce an exact answer for the computation time of tasks, however frequently it may be able to provide upper and lower bounds on the computation time. If such information is available, our technique can exploit it to produce a higher utilization bound.

Also, our technique is applicable to any arbitrary fixed priority assignment, and to situations where some tasks must be complete before, at or after the end of their periods, in which case the Liu and Layland bound [l] is not applicable.

Thus these inequalities simply state that at each task arrival in [0, Dij] there should be no idle time.
The linear programming process finds a set of computation times whose combined utilization is minimal, and such that there is no idle time [8].

The only time these inequalities will create a difficulty is when minimum and/or maximum times have been specified for all of the tasks currently under consideration. We take care of this special case by checking explicitly for it in the procedure described later. In all other cases, linear programming will vary the computation time which is not bounded in such a way as to satisfy the inequalities.
Thus, we can determine the bounds by iteratively applying linear programming to each deadline of each task. We formalize this into a procedure in the next section.

Our technique results that task 72 has a bound of 83.33%. This bound occurs when the computation times of 71 and 72 are 100 and 200. Similarly, we show the bounds for 73 and 74, and the corresponding worst-case computation times. Of course, the computation times of lower priority tasks are irrelevant in determining the bound for higher priority tasks. The table illustrates that 74 is safe as long as the system utilization is below 98.37%. The 72 may be threatened if utilization of 7 1 and 72 exceeds 83.33%. Also, task 5 may be threatened if combined utilization of T I , 72 and 73 exceeds 83.07%. Thus, all tasks are guaranteed to meet their deadlines if their combined processor utilization is equal to or less than 83.07%.

Table 2 shows the results of some simulation studies for determining task set-specific utilization bounds for randomly generated task sets. Task periods were uniformly distributed between 20 and 2400. The table shows the B, for the several task sets generated, with computation time not available and available. It should be noted that uniform distributions are not likely to produce task sets with harmonic frequencies, particularly for large task sets. In contrast, in real systems, frequencies are multiples of some basic clock cycle, hence they do tend to be harmonic and clustered.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we presented a technique for determining task set-specific utilization bounds for fixedpriority real-time scheduling. Our technique fills an important gap between the Liu and Layland's schedulability test which does not take specific task information into account, and exact schedulability tests, which require complete information about the task set. Sys- tem designers can use this technique to obtain a better check of scheduling feasibility. An additional major benefit of our technique is that it opens up an alternative approach based on linear programming to analyzing the behavior of fixed-priority scheduling. We are optimistic about the potential of this approach because of its extensibility to a variety of scheduling problems.
